People expect this work to be dramatic and it almost never is. In fifteen years I have opened a great many files and found a conspiracy perhaps twice. What I find the rest of the time is an email that somebody read on a Friday, a control that was written down and never tested, and an audit that got moved twice because the quarter was busy. If that audit had gone ahead the first time it was scheduled, most of these cases would not exist. That is not a comforting thing to tell a board, because a conspiracy is somebody else's fault and a postponed audit is theirs. The sentence I have said most often in my career is this: nothing was concealed here, nobody looked. And if somebody had been given four hours and permission, they would have found it in an afternoon.

The cheapest lesson any organisation ever gets is the one where nothing happened. Somebody notices a payment that should not have been possible, it gets stopped, and the whole thing is over in a morning. That is a free education, and almost nobody takes it, because there is no damage to explain and therefore no meeting. If we treated near misses the way aviation does, half of what I work on would never reach me. Aviation writes them up whether or not anybody was hurt, and the write-up goes to people who were not involved. We do the opposite: we investigate in proportion to the harm, so the only lessons that get learned are the expensive ones. If our industry had adopted that habit twenty years ago, the fines we are still paying for would look very different. It costs nothing. That is precisely why it never gets funded.

A rule exists, and a process is written down to apply it. The audit that would have tested that process is scheduled and then postponed twice. A red flag arrives and sits in the queue of somebody with four hundred other things to read. Eighteen months later the regulator finds it, and nothing had been concealed at any point. A fine is paid, nobody admits wrongdoing, and the reputational damage has no number attached to it.
